newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - Stronger even without Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - Stronger even without Iraq.

text.p: European oil products were expected to jump higher this week as delays to Iraqi crude exports give an extra kick to the already strong market, traders said.

On Sunday the U.N. delayed the Iraqi oil-for-food deal after Baghdad's troops attacked the northern town of Arbil. Iraq was expected to begin exporting crude oil and products this month building to about 550,000 barrels per day at current prices.
Gas oil will remain the driving force due to low stocks, the introduction of tough new green rules and strong demand for jet fuel, dealers said.
After hitting five year highs soon after the open on Monday IPE gas oil showed no sign of weakness.
September traded around $205 a tonne. Dealers saw an upside target of $226 on the nearby IPE contract, which traded in the winter after the Gulf War.
Physical gas oil commanded big premiums. The new 0.05 percent sulphur diesel grade, due to be introduced Europe-wide next month, asked some $12 above IPE levels.
In addition, dealers said they expected good demand from Germany for heating oil this week as consumers look to stock up ahead of the winter.

Consultants Petroleum Finance company said in an August report: "German (heating oil) tertiary stocks remain at record low levels... a late August-September rush to fill consumers' tanks could spark price increases in Europe."

Last week's API data showed U.S. distillate stocks nearly 20 million barrels below year-ago levels, and European inventories are similarly lower. Jet prices added to the tightness of middle distillates with strong Asian demand and big premiums being discussed in Europe.
"A lot of the airlines didn't buy in the spring due to the high prices and the chance of Iraq coming back," a trader said.
"But they got caught and are buying now for the winter," he added.
Gasoline was well supported.
Regular gasoline barges in the ARA region were worth around $200 a tonne - unusually, just less than gas oil prices. Supply is scarce due to refinery maintenance and low crude runs.
Traders only saw around three cargoes available for prompt loading which could be sold to the U.S.
Naphtha was also fairly tight, although a steady trickle of small Russian pieces kept the lid on prices.
A six-week rolling programme of closures at the Skikda refinery will also tightening markets.
High sulphur fuel oil is tight and good demand is expected for product to fill the latest Portuguese tender.
Portugal's state utility EdP tendered to buy up to eight 20,000 tonne cargoes for delivery in September and October last week. Low sulphur fuel was also expected to remain firm.
Although the main Mediterranean buyer has kept a low profile over the last month, many traders feel they have been discreetly buying spot cargoes.
-- Nicholas Shaxson, London newsroom +44 171 542 8167
